newsitem.title: USA: O'Leary to quit U.S. Energy Department.
newsitem.headline: O'Leary to quit U.S. Energy Department.

text.p: Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary confirmed on Wednesday that she was resigning but would not reveal her future plans.

O'Leary has spent the last two years under siege, with Republicans battling to dismantle the Energy Department and attacking the secretary for her extensive foreign trips to promote U.S. business deals.

The secretary had long said she did not plan to stay for more than one term, although after beating back congressional attempts to get rid of the Energy Department she once said she felt emboldened to stay on.
Brought in from an electric utility, Northern States Power, O'Leary was one of the few energy secretaries who had energy industry experience.
"We could do a lot worse, as far as the industry is concerned," said Urvan Sternfels, president of the National Petroleum Refiners Association.
"She has had her problems, but she also understands ... that when there are political concerns about supply and price, there is a marketplace out there that works that out pretty well," he said.

He was referring to two episodes this year, when the administration was pressured by lawmakers to do something about soaring gasoline and heating oil prices. In both cases, O'Leary refused to step into the market to cap prices or bolster supplies.

O'Leary considers one of her biggest accomplishments to be the opening up of long-secret government documents on human radiation experiments conducted during the Cold War, which resulted in a report last year calling for compensation of victims who were harmed in tests done without their knowledge.
Names most widely rumoured as replacements for O'Leary include Deputy Secretary Charles Curtis and Representative Bill Richardson, a New Mexico Democrat.
An Energy Department official said if Curtis was offered the job, "he would take it."
Richardson had no immediate comment on whether he was interested in the job.
